title: Chapter XIV

teacherSummary.text: The creature learns the De Laceys' history: Felix helped Safie's father, a Turkish merchant, escape unjust execution in Paris; the merchant betrayed them, and the family lost wealth and was exiled. Safie fled to find Felix.

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: Excerpt-based (Middle School support track; this novel is above the grades 6–8 complexity band, so work from the passage your teacher selects). In “Chapter XIV,” how does Shelley show injustice and exile? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the passage, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the plot you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: HS Freshman
writingPrompts.text: In Chapter XIV, how does Shelley develop the idea of injustice and exile? State a clear claim, support it with two or three quotations, and explain how the plot in the chapter helps build that idea.

writingPrompts.label: HS Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Chapter XIV develops the idea of injustice and exile. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of plot and characterization shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: HS Junior
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how the structure of Chapter XIV (where it begins, turns and ends) and its plot shape the reader's understanding of injustice and exile. Identify one place where the text leaves matters uncertain and explain how that uncertainty adds to its meaning.

writingPrompts.label: HS Senior
writingPrompts.text: Two readers disagree about what Chapter XIV suggests about injustice and exile. Lay out two plausible interpretations, weigh the evidence for each (including the chapter's plot and characterization), and argue for the stronger one in a sustained, well-organized essay.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Mary Shelley uses plot in Chapter XIV to complicate the reader's understanding of injustice and exile. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Chapter XIV within its historical and literary context and argue how the chapter's treatment of injustice and exile responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: College Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Read Chapter XIV alongside the conventions of its genre and period. Argue how the chapter's handling of injustice and exile follows or bends those conventions, using the plot as evidence, and test your reading against one published critic. Document two secondary sources in MLA.

writingPrompts.label: College Junior
writingPrompts.text: Apply a named critical approach (for example formalist, historicist, feminist, psychoanalytic or ecocritical) to Chapter XIV and its treatment of injustice and exile. State your method, show what it reveals in the chapter's plot and characterization, and identify where the text resists it.

writingPrompts.label: College Senior
writingPrompts.text: Develop a research argument that reads Chapter XIV as evidence for a larger claim about injustice and exile in Frankenstein. Connect close reading of the chapter to the whole novel, engage at least four scholarly sources, and state precisely where your reading departs from theirs (Chicago style).

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Chapter XIV as a hinge in the novel's larger treatment of injustice and exile. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Frankenstein.

segments.activity: Respond in writing to the bell-ringer, then pair-share.
segments.script: Settle in and write for five minutes: How does the De Laceys' story parallel the creature's own situation? No wrong answers yet; we will test these ideas against the text. Two volunteers share, and I note key words on the board. Before we start, a content note: The chapter continues stereotypes about Safie's father.

segments.activity: Introduce 5 key words: pronounce, define from context, then the word's history.
segments.script: Today's words are facilitated, reiterating, expostulate, passports, noisome. For each one we read the sentence, guess from context and then check the definition. Here is the first: “His plans were facilitated by the news which arrived from Paris.” In this sentence it means: made easier. Word histories: “expostulate”: From Latin expostulare "to demand urgently, remonstrate," from ex- + postulare "to demand." For the other words, look up the word history (Etymonline or the OED) and record the language of origin and the root meaning in your etymology log.

segments.activity: Present the historical and literary background.
segments.script: Here is what the first readers of Frankenstein would have known. The story reflects prejudices and politics of 18th-century France and attitudes toward the Ottoman world. Why does this chapter matter? Injustice repeats across the book; the virtuous suffer, and betrayal is common. Write down one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Teacher models a think-aloud on the anchor passage for plot.
segments.script: Watch me read this the way a careful reader does. The passage opens: ““The name of the old man was De Lacey.” I stop and ask: what is the author doing here, and how does it connect to injustice and exile? I circle “affluence”, one of today's words, and ask why the author chose it over a plainer word. When I find plot, I underline it and write its effect in the margin, then I check my idea against the next sentence.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for plot.
segments.script: Now we do it together. I read the first sentence and you track along. Mark every example of plot. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice? I will collect three ideas and we choose the strongest using evidence.

segments.activity: Students annotate a new passage independently in the reader, then begin the writing prompt at their assigned rigor level.
segments.script: Your turn. Annotate the next page in the app for Plot, Characterization, Irony: at least three marks with a margin note each. Then open your writing prompt; the app shows the level your teacher assigned (for a 9–10 class, the HS Sophomore prompt reads: Analyze how Chapter XIV develops the idea of injustice and exile. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of plot and characterization shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.) I will circulate and conference.

segments.activity: Structured discussion (think-pair-share or a short Socratic circle).
segments.script: Let's talk. Our question: How does this chapter connect to the costs of unchecked ambition? Every claim needs a page reference. Respond to the person before you by agreeing, extending or challenging with evidence.

segments.activity: Chapter quiz in the app, then a one-sentence exit ticket.
segments.script: Take the chapter quiz in the app. Then, in one sentence, tell me what this chapter suggests about injustice and exile, backed by one short quotation.

segments.activity: Summarize the lesson and preview the next reading.
segments.script: Today we saw how plot shapes injustice and exile. Tonight, read the next chapter and add two words to your etymology log.
